title: AI assistant for podcast producers on Mac in 2026: guest prep, show notes and edits
metaTitle: AI Assistant for Podcast Producers on Mac | Lazur
description: Lazur is an AI assistant for podcast producers on Mac. Hold a key to ask about your screen, draft show notes, research guests and get edit help.
secondaryKeywords: podcast editing with AI on Mac
intro: An AI assistant for podcast producers on Mac should work in the apps you already open, such as Zoom, Descript, Google Docs and Gmail. Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that works that way. Hold ⌥ ⌘, ask about what is on your screen, and it answers out loud and points at the thing you mean. It guides you and drafts text. It does not click or edit for you.
tldr: Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and it answers out loud.
It helps with guest research, show notes, titles and questions inside the apps you already use.
It guides you one click at a time. It does not click, edit or publish for you.
Public data on producer time is thin. The best figure is 55% spending 1 to 5 hours per episode, with no sample size given.
Check your guest agreements and your employer's rules before you paste guest details into any tool.

blocks.text: Podcast producers rarely have a job title that matches the work. You book the guest, read the bio, write the show notes, cut the dead air and push a clip to social. Most of that happens on a Mac, across many apps, often in a single day. The useful question is which of those minutes an assistant can give back.
Where a podcast producer's day goes

The best public number I found covers the whole episode, not the day. The 2025 Independent Podcast Report found that 55% of respondents spend 1 to 5 hours per episode, from planning through publishing. Another 13% spend more than ten hours. The page gives no sample size, and its bands add up to only 72%. Read it as a rough picture, not a rule for your show.

No sourced survey ranks the tasks that take the most time for podcast producers. None splits an episode between email, editing and admin either. Your own time log will tell you more than any report. The rest of this page sticks to what the sources say, and marks where they stop.
Mac apps producers use, and what the sources say

Castos surveyed 99 creators in March 2026 and published the results in May. The respondents were Castos's own customers, so the sample is not neutral. The tool answers are still useful. Audacity was the top editing tool by a significant margin. Adobe Audition and GarageBand or Logic Pro tied for second. Descript had what Castos calls a real foothold, with several creators using it as their main editor.

Audacity's Mac download page lists version 4.0.2. It offers an ARM64 disk image for Apple silicon and says the app is tested on macOS 14 and 15. The same page says there is no plugin support. If your edit depends on a plugin chain, test that before you switch.

Descript's changelog lists a release roundup dated November 6, 2026. Recent entries include saved workflows you can call as slash commands, a 30-day project trash, and alerts during recording when a camera, screen share or microphone goes dead. That last alert matters when a remote guest's mic dies mid-call.

Riverside's help article, dated September 7, 2026, says the full Riverside Editor now runs inside the native Mac app. You can edit without leaving your desktop. The article does not give a macOS requirement, so check the requirements on Riverside's site before you install.

blocks.text: Look at the right-hand column. Lazur does not edit audio in any of these tools. It explains what you see, points at the control and walks you through the steps. You still do the clicking, and you stay in control of the file.
Episode workflow from plan to publish
An episode moves through a few stages: plan, prep, record, edit and publish. Lazur helps most where you lose time to a question, not to typing. Each stage below shows the kind of question that works.
Planning and guest prep

Start with the guest. Ask Lazur to research their recent interviews. It runs the search in its own Chrome tabs, through the Lazur for Chrome extension, and returns a summary and a report. Open the links it names and check every fact. A bio can read well and still be out of date.
Recording on a Mac

Recording is where the Mac can fail quietly. Set the input before the call. Go to System Settings > Sound > Input and pick the right microphone. Then start a backup. QuickTime Player > File > New Audio Recording gives you a second file in a few clicks. Ask Lazur to explain the input level if the meter looks wrong. It explains, but it does not change the setting.
Editing

Editing takes the most time once the file exists. Describe the moment you want, such as the part where the guest explains the first job, and ask Lazur to point at it. It circles the waveform or paragraph and adds a label. Then you cut. The circle saves you from scrubbing the timeline.

Edge cases matter here. A remote guest's audio can drift from your local track, so check the sync at the first laugh and again at the end. Name files with the guest and the date before you export, so a clip never sits next to the wrong episode. If a sync or naming dialog appears, ask Lazur to explain it. Then make the change yourself.
Publishing

Publishing is mostly forms: a title, a description, tags and a caption for each clip. This is where dictation helps. Hold fn, speak the rough version, and the text lands at the cursor in any app. Then ask Lazur to tighten it. Dictation is unlimited on both Pro and Power, and Snippets save your show boilerplate.
Worked example: one guest from booking to show notes
Here is one guest, start to finish, with the words you would say. The guest is booked for next week. You already have their email and a bio link.

items: Booking: say 'Add the recording to my Calendar for next Tuesday at 10:00.' Lazur adds the Calendar event.
Research: say 'Research their last few interviews and list the links.' Lazur runs it in Chrome tabs and comes back with a summary and a report.
Questions: say 'Draft questions from that summary. Plain language, no yes or no questions.' Lazur drafts the questions as text you can paste into your doc.
Recording: check System Settings > Sound > Input, then start QuickTime Player > File > New Audio Recording as a backup.
During the call: hold fn and dictate timestamps. Say the time and a few words, and the text lands at the cursor.
Show notes: say 'Draft show notes from this transcript and keep quotes exact.' Then check each quote against the audio.

blocks.text: The order matters. Research comes before questions, and questions come before the call. Show notes come last, once the audio is clean and the timestamps exist. That order avoids doing the same work twice.
Show notes, titles and guest research with an AI assistant

Use an AI assistant for the wordy parts: a first draft of show notes, a short list of title options, a plain bio. The output still needs your check. A model can invent a book title, a date or a link. Compare every name, number and link with the guest's own pages before you publish.

A common mistake is pasting a full transcript and asking for everything at once. Split the job. Ask for timestamps in one pass, the notes in another and the titles last. Smaller tasks are easier to check, and you spot errors sooner.
If you prefer a chat window for this work, read [ChatGPT for podcast producers on Mac](/for/podcast-producers/chatgpt). It covers show notes, titles and guest research in one place.
Video clips and the extra export

Video changes the job. Castos reports that 34% of creators record video for every episode, and 16% record video for some episodes. Of the video creators, 82% publish to YouTube and 46% post social clips. Each video route adds an export, a caption and an upload.

The common mistake is exporting the full episode first, then finding out the clip needs a different shape. Decide the clip format before you export. Ask Lazur to explain the crop or aspect setting in your editor, and to point at it. Then you choose.
Email, calendar and interruptions

Microsoft's Work Trend Index 2025 survey reports 117 emails a day for the average worker. Microsoft also says employees are interrupted 'every two minutes during core work hours'. These are general office figures, not podcast data. No podcast-specific study sets a number for producers' email. Treat them as a warning, not a measure of your inbox.

Sort guest email before you read it. In Gmail, click the gear icon, then go to See all settings > Filters and Blocked Addresses. The step by step is in [how to create a filter in Gmail](/how-to/create-a-filter-in-gmail). Pair it with [how to create a label in Gmail](/how-to/create-a-label-in-gmail) so guest threads sit in one place.

Use Apple Reminders for the follow-ups a filter cannot catch. Say 'Remind me at 10:30 to send the guest questions,' and Lazur adds the reminder. A booked recording can go in Calendar the same way. Keep each follow-up in the app you check first.
What about privacy and guest data

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Those are product facts. They do not replace your own duties to a guest or an employer.

blocks.title: Guest data comes first
blocks.text: Some guests sign confidentiality terms, and some employers set data rules. Follow your employer's rules and your contracts before you paste a private email, a medical story or a legal detail into any tool. This page makes no compliance claims for Lazur.
Mistakes producers make with AI on a Mac

items: Asking for the whole episode in one request. Split the job, then check each piece.
Trusting a name, date or link because it sounds right. Check it against the source.
Waiting for Lazur to finish an export. Lazur guides you one click at a time, and you press each button yourself.
Skipping the backup recording because the notes look fine. A note cannot replace audio that was never recorded.
Dictating into the wrong window. Click into the document first, then hold fn.
Pasting a guest's private contact details into a prompt when you do not need them. Remove them first.

Setting up Lazur for your producer work
Setup takes a few minutes. Start with the download page, then learn two shortcuts. The rest comes as you use it.

items: Download Lazur from [the download page](/download). It runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and on Intel.
Open the app. The Pro trial starts when you first open it, and it needs no credit card.
Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask about anything on screen. Lazur answers out loud.
Hold fn to dictate. Text appears at the cursor in any app.
Add Snippets for your show intro and a personal dictionary for guest names.
Compare plans on [the pricing page](/pricing) before you decide.

blocks.text: Give Lazur a short test first. Pick one task from your last episode, run it, and check the output against the source. If it saves you time and the check is quick, keep it. If the check takes longer than the task, drop it.
What to do next

Start with the longest task in your last episode. Time it once with a timer, or ask Lazur to start one. Then run the same task with Lazur and time it again. Your own numbers will tell you more than any average. If your guests record remotely, read the [Zoom guide for podcast producers](/for/podcast-producers/zoom) next.

faq.question: What is an AI assistant for podcast producers on Mac?
faq.answer: It is an assistant that sees what is on your screen and answers out loud. Lazur is one example. You hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen. It can research guests, draft show notes, explain dialogs in your editor and dictate text at the cursor. It does not edit your audio for you.

faq.question: Does Lazur edit audio, upload episodes or click buttons for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. It points at things, explains them and guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. It also drafts and types text. You keep control of every file and every publish button.

faq.question: Does Lazur work inside Zoom, Riverside or Descript?
faq.answer: It is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and it has no partnership with any app maker. It works next to the apps you already use. Hold ⌥ ⌘ while the app is in front and ask your question. For recording setup, read the Zoom guide for podcast producers on this site.

faq.question: Is my guest's audio sent to an AI company?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Check your guest agreements before you share any recording with a tool.

faq.question: Can I put confidential guest or client details into it?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules and your contracts first. Some guest and client details carry duties that a product note cannot settle. This page makes no compliance claims for Lazur. When in doubt, remove names and contact details before you ask.

faq.question: Does it work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. A Windows version is planned, but it is not available. If your edit suite runs on Windows, you can still use Lazur on a Mac for research and show notes.

faq.question: How is it different from ChatGPT?
faq.answer: Lazur is built around your Mac screen and your voice. You hold ⌥ ⌘, ask about what is in front of you, and it answers out loud. Compare any tool on what it can see, what it stores and what it costs before you decide.

faq.question: Does Lazur remember what I did?
faq.answer: Lazur keeps a memory of what you asked and did, on your Mac. Use it to find an answer you got last week. Check the source again before you rely on a remembered fact, because the memory is only as good as the check you made at the time.

faq.question: What does Lazur cost?
faq.answer: Lazur has a Pro trial that needs no credit card. Paid plans are Pro and Power, with different limits on AI actions. See the pricing page for current prices, since prices can change.

painPoints.title: Episode time runs long
painPoints.text: More than half of respondents in one 2025 survey spend 1 to 5 hours per episode, from planning through publishing. That survey gives no sample size, so use it as a rough guide, not a benchmark.

painPoints.title: Too many apps for one episode
painPoints.text: Editing can span Audacity, Descript, Riverside, Adobe Audition, GarageBand or Logic Pro. Audacity led the Castos survey by a significant margin, but the rest of the field is spread out. Each app has its own menus to learn.

painPoints.title: Video adds a second publish
painPoints.text: Castos found that 34% of creators record video for every episode. Of video creators, 82% publish to YouTube and 46% post social clips. Each format needs its own export, caption and upload.

painPoints.title: Guest research eats prep time
painPoints.text: Reading a guest's past work takes time, and it is easy to miss a detail. No public source measures this for producers. Your own time log is the best way to see whether research is your biggest cost.

painPoints.title: Email and interruptions fill the gaps
painPoints.text: Microsoft reports 117 emails a day for the average knowledge worker. That figure is general office data, not podcast data. It still shows how fast a guest thread can bury the one message you need.
